tagline: An old turnpike corridor connects stone walls, schools and summer houses.
intro: Connecticut’s Route 169 byway winds past stone walls, colonial houses and meetinghouses, with maple and pine stands and glacial boulders scattered through fields. The Federal Highway Administration lists this National Scenic Byway as 32 miles and allows an hour for the drive, or a full day with visits. Its description emphasizes the historic buildings linking New England towns.

The Norwich and Woodstock Turnpike began as a private toll road incorporated in 1801; its corporation dissolved in 1846. From Kinsman Hill Road, the turnpike followed the later Route 169 alignment north to Woodstock and the Massachusetts line. Much of that route became Route 93 in 1932, then Route 169 in 1959 to free the earlier number for Interstate 93. State scenic designation followed in 1991, and national designation in 1996.

Start at the Massachusetts line and head south through Woodstock, Pomfret, Brooklyn and Canterbury toward Lisbon. Woodstock’s Roseland Cottage is a Gothic Revival summer house on Route 169. Pomfret Street’s historic district includes two private schools. At Brooklyn, Putnam’s equestrian monument stands south of the town green. Through Canterbury, the highway runs parallel to the Quinebaug River without following its bank. The designated corridor ends at Rocky Hollow Road in Lisbon; the numbered highway continues beyond it to Norwich.

moments.title: Roseland Cottage, Woodstock
moments.text: Roseland Cottage’s coral-pink exterior belongs to a Gothic Revival summer house built in 1846 for Henry Chandler Bowen and his family. Architect Joseph C. Wells designed the house under Bowen’s direction. The house retains original Gothic furniture and embossed wall decoration. Its garden preserves an 1850 arrangement of twenty-one flowerbeds bordered by boxwood. The complex also includes an icehouse, a carriage barn and an indoor bowling alley. Writer and designer Andrew Jackson Downing’s principles shaped the ensemble, joining practical concerns with picturesque design. Historic New England owns the house and operates it as a museum.

moments.title: Brooklyn
moments.text: Israel Putnam points forward from a bronze horse just south of Brooklyn’s town green. The monument is also his tomb: his remains were reinterred beneath it when it was completed. Dedicated in 1888, the statue was designed by Karl Gerhardt to honor the Revolutionary War general. An oval base ringed with bronze oak leaves supports the statue. A granite pedestal supports the horse and rider. Putnam wears a tricorne and carries a sword at his left side; the horse raises its left foreleg. One pedestal inscription repeats the words from the cover of his original tomb.

moments.title: Prudence Crandall Museum, Canterbury
moments.text: The house on Canterbury’s village green became a school where the admission of Sarah Harris, a Black student, prompted white parents to withdraw their daughters. She had purchased the vacant house in 1831, paying part of its price through a mortgage. Prudence Crandall reopened it for African-American students in 1833. Canterbury residents opposed the school, then used violence when legal efforts did not quickly close it. Crandall closed it in 1834 to protect her students. The house is now a museum with period rooms and changing exhibits. Its original stairway and ornamental fireplace mantel survive inside.
